```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center", dpi = 110)
```

This notebook segments customers in two settings:

- **A. Hotel guests** (behavioural data, all numeric): which guest segments bring in the most lodging and ancillary revenue, and how should the hotel target them?
- **B. Users of a social app** (demographic data, mostly categorical): what user types exist?

Part B also shows a common pitfall. Running k-means on one-hot encoded categorical variables lets a single binary variable drive the clustering. The result is then compared with a method designed for mixed data: Gower distance with PAM (k-medoids).

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(factoextra)
library(cluster)
library(knitr)
set.seed(123)

# share of each variable's variance explained by the clustering (between-cluster SS / total SS)
separation <- function(X, cl) {
  X <- as.data.frame(X)
  sapply(X, function(x) 1 - sum(tapply(x, cl, function(v) sum((v - mean(v))^2))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2))
}
```

# A. Hotel guests

## A1. Data

The data is a sample of 10,001 customers of a Lisbon hotel (Antonio, de Almeida & Nunes, 2020, *Data in Brief*). Customers with a missing or implausible age (under 18 or over 95) are removed. Segmentation uses nine behavioural variables.

```{r hotel_data}
hotel <- read.csv("data/HotelCustomersSubset_sample.csv") |>
  mutate(Age = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Age))) |>
  filter(!is.na(Age), Age >= 18, Age <= 95)

seg_vars <- c("Age", "AverageLeadTime", "DaysSinceCreation", "LodgingRevenue", "OtherRevenue",
              "PersonsNights", "RoomNights", "DaysSinceLastStay", "DaysSinceFirstStay")
cat(nrow(hotel), "customers after cleaning\n")
summary(hotel[seg_vars])
```

Two things matter before clustering:
- **The variables are on very different scales.** Euros, days and counts all appear, and k-means uses Euclidean distance. All variables are therefore standardised.
- **Three variables measure almost the same thing.** Most customers stayed only once, so "days since first stay", "days since last stay" and "days since account creation" are nearly identical. Tenure therefore counts about three times in the distance:

```{r hotel_corr}
round(cor(hotel[, c("DaysSinceCreation", "DaysSinceLastStay", "DaysSinceFirstStay")]), 3)
```

## A2. How many clusters?

The silhouette is computed on a random subsample of 3,000 customers. A full distance matrix for 9,000+ customers would need several GB of memory.

```{r hotel_k, fig.height=3.5}
hotel_scaled <- scale(hotel[seg_vars])
sub <- hotel_scaled[sample(nrow(hotel_scaled), 3000), ]
fviz_nbclust(hotel_scaled, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 12, nstart = 10) + labs(title = "Elbow method")
fviz_nbclust(sub, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 12, nstart = 10) + labs(title = "Silhouette (3,000-customer subsample)")
wss <- sapply(1:8, function(k) { set.seed(123); kmeans(hotel_scaled, k, nstart = 10, iter.max = 50)$tot.withinss })
tibble(k = 2:8, `drop in within-cluster SS` = -diff(wss)) |> kable(digits = 0)
```

There is no sharp elbow. Each extra cluster still reduces the within-cluster sum of squares, but the gains level off: the drop from 4 to 5 clusters is about half the drop from 2 to 3, and it falls again after that. Four segments are also a manageable number for marketing actions, so **k = 4** is used. It is run with 25 random starts (`nstart = 25`), because a single start can get stuck in a poor local optimum.

## A3. Four-segment solution

```{r hotel_kmeans}
set.seed(123)
km_hotel <- kmeans(hotel_scaled, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
hotel$cluster <- factor(km_hotel$cluster)

profile <- hotel |> group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(customers = n(), across(all_of(seg_vars), mean),
            total_lodging = sum(LodgingRevenue), total_other = sum(OtherRevenue)) |>
  mutate(share_customers = customers / sum(customers),
         share_lodging = total_lodging / sum(total_lodging),
         share_other = total_other / sum(total_other))
profile |> select(cluster, customers, Age, AverageLeadTime, RoomNights, PersonsNights,
                  LodgingRevenue, OtherRevenue, DaysSinceLastStay) |>
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "Segment profiles (means)")
```

```{r hotel_plots, fig.height=3.5}
fviz_cluster(km_hotel, data = hotel_scaled, geom = "point", ellipse.type = "norm", pointsize = 0.6,
             ggtheme = theme_minimal(), main = "Hotel segments (first two principal components)")

profile |> select(cluster, `average lodging revenue (€)` = LodgingRevenue, `average other revenue (€)` = OtherRevenue) |>
  pivot_longer(-cluster) |>
  ggplot(aes(cluster, value, fill = cluster)) + geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free_y") + theme_minimal() + labs(x = "segment", y = NULL)
```

**Average vs total revenue.** The segment with the highest revenue *per customer* is not necessarily the one with the most revenue *in total*. Targeting decisions need both:

```{r hotel_share}
profile |> transmute(cluster, `share of customers` = share_customers,
                     `share of lodging revenue` = share_lodging, `share of other revenue` = share_other) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r hotel_separation}
sort(round(separation(hotel_scaled, km_hotel$cluster), 2), decreasing = TRUE)
```

The table above shows the share of each variable's variance that the segmentation explains. The segments are mostly defined by **tenure** (the three day-count variables), **stay length and revenue**, and **booking lead time**. Age plays a smaller role.

## A4. Robustness: the effect of skewed revenue

Revenue and nights are strongly right-skewed: lodging revenue has a mean of about €365 and a maximum of about €7,500. In Euclidean distance, a few very large spenders can pull a centroid towards them. Re-running k-means on log-transformed versions shows how much the segments depend on this.

```{r hotel_log}
skewed <- c("AverageLeadTime", "LodgingRevenue", "OtherRevenue", "PersonsNights", "RoomNights")
hotel_log <- hotel[seg_vars] |> mutate(across(all_of(skewed), log1p)) |> scale()
set.seed(123)
km_log <- kmeans(hotel_log, centers = 4, nstart = 25)

adjusted_rand <- function(a, b) {
  t <- table(a, b); n <- sum(t); s <- function(x) sum(choose(x, 2))
  expected <- s(rowSums(t)) * s(colSums(t)) / choose(n, 2)
  (s(t) - expected) / ((s(rowSums(t)) + s(colSums(t))) / 2 - expected)
}
table(original = km_hotel$cluster, `log-transformed` = km_log$cluster)
cat(sprintf("Adjusted Rand index between the two solutions: %.2f (1 = identical, 0 = chance agreement)\n",
            adjusted_rand(km_hotel$cluster, km_log$cluster)))
```

The agreement is low (ARI ≈ 0.27). Most of the high-value segment (segment 2) merges with segment 1 on the log scale. That segment is therefore defined by the **long tail of large spenders**. For revenue targeting this is acceptable, because the tail is exactly what management cares about. But the segment boundaries depend on how revenue is scaled, and they should be presented as indicative rather than as fixed customer "types".

## A5. What this means for the hotel

**The four segments:**
- **Segment 2: high-value long stays.** 11% of guests, but **53% of lodging and 54% of ancillary revenue**. Guests stay about 6.5 room nights with about 15 person-nights, so they are often groups or families, and they book about 110 days ahead.
- **Segment 4: older early planners.** Average age 66, booking about 250 days ahead. Lodging revenue is average, but ancillary spend is relatively high: €100 against €260 lodging, the highest ratio of the four segments.
- **Segments 1 and 3: short, low-spend stays.** Together 73% of guests. They differ mainly in how long ago they became customers.

**Two recommendations:**
1. **Target segment 2 with retention and pre-arrival upselling.** One in ten guests brings in half the revenue, so keeping them matters more than finding new ones. The long booking horizon leaves time for pre-arrival offers such as room upgrades, family suites and dining packages, and for direct-booking incentives that cut commission costs on the most valuable stays.
2. **Position spa and dining packages for segment 4.** These guests plan far ahead and already spend proportionally more on extras. Early-booking packages that bundle the room with F&B or spa credit fit their behaviour. They can be marketed at the time of booking, months before the stay.

# B. Social-app users: k-means vs Gower + PAM

## B1. Data

There are 1,113 users of a social networking app:
- **Binary:** sex, marital status.
- **Categorical:** education, occupation, town size, sports-fan type.
- **Numeric:** age, income, number of children.

```{r app_data}
load("data/CustomerSegmentation.RData")   # data frame `df`
app <- df
str(app)
app |> summarise(across(c(age, income, children), list(mean = mean, sd = sd))) |> kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r app_eda, fig.height=3.2}
app |> select(age, income, children) |> pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "skyblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free") + theme_minimal() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

## B2. k-means on one-hot encoded data

This is the standard recipe: log-transform income, one-hot encode the categories, standardise everything, then run k-means. The elbow and silhouette both point to **k = 3**.

```{r app_kmeans, fig.height=3.5}
app_num <- app |> mutate(income = log1p(income))
dummies <- as.data.frame(model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = app_num))
dummies <- dummies[, apply(dummies, 2, var) > 0]
app_scaled <- scale(dummies)

fviz_nbclust(app_scaled, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 10, nstart = 10) + labs(title = "Silhouette: k-means on one-hot data")
set.seed(123)
km_app <- kmeans(app_scaled, centers = 3, nstart = 25)

profile_app <- function(cl) app |> mutate(cluster = factor(cl)) |> group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(users = n(), age = mean(age), income = mean(income), children = mean(children),
            `% female` = 100 * mean(sex == "1"), `% married` = 100 * mean(married == "1"))
profile_app(km_app$cluster) |> kable(digits = 1, caption = "k-means segments (k = 3)")
```

**The problem.** Two of the three segments are 100% one sex. Which variables drive the split?

```{r app_kmeans_driver}
sort(round(separation(app_scaled, km_app$cluster), 2), decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

Each k-means segment is essentially **one dummy column**:
- segment 1 is the users with the highest education levels (`education2/3`);
- segments 2 and 3 are everyone else, split exactly by sex.

```{r app_kmeans_check}
table(`k-means segment` = km_app$cluster, education = app$education)
table(`k-means segment` = km_app$cluster, sex = app$sex)
```

The reason is mechanical. A standardised 0/1 variable is far from the mean for *every* observation (about ±1 SD), while a continuous variable is far from its mean only for its extreme values. So binary dummies contribute large, constant distances, and k-means is drawn to split along them. Each extra dummy column of a categorical variable also adds weight to that variable. The "segments" here are partly an artefact of the encoding.

## B3. Gower distance + PAM

**Gower distance** handles mixed data directly:
- numeric variables contribute their range-normalised absolute difference;
- categorical variables contribute 0 if two users match and 1 if they differ;
- every variable gets the same weight, regardless of how many levels it has.

**PAM** (partitioning around medoids) clusters on any distance matrix, and its cluster centres are real users (medoids).

```{r app_gower, fig.height=3.5}
gower <- daisy(app, metric = "gower")
sil_width <- sapply(2:8, function(k) pam(gower, k = k, diss = TRUE)$silinfo$avg.width)
tibble(k = 2:8, `average silhouette` = sil_width) |>
  ggplot(aes(k, `average silhouette`)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Silhouette: PAM on Gower distance")
k_best <- (2:8)[which.max(sil_width)]
cat("best k by silhouette:", k_best, "\n")
```

```{r app_pam}
pam_app <- pam(gower, k = k_best, diss = TRUE)
profile_app(pam_app$clustering) |> kable(digits = 1, caption = sprintf("PAM segments (k = %d)", k_best))

app[pam_app$medoids, ] |> mutate(cluster = seq_len(k_best), .before = 1) |>
  kable(caption = "Medoids: the most representative user of each segment")

pam_drivers <- sapply(app, function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) summary(aov(x ~ factor(pam_app$clustering)))[[1]][1, "Sum Sq"] / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
  else as.numeric(chisq.test(table(x, pam_app$clustering))$statistic) / (length(x) * (min(nlevels(factor(x)), k_best) - 1))
})
sort(round(pam_drivers, 2), decreasing = TRUE)
```

The final table shows the strength of each variable's association with the PAM segments: R² for numeric variables and Cramér's V² for categorical ones.

```{r app_compare}
table(`k-means` = km_app$cluster, PAM = pam_app$clustering)
cat(sprintf("Adjusted Rand index k-means vs PAM: %.2f\n", adjusted_rand(km_app$cluster, pam_app$clustering)))
```

**Is the sex split then just an artefact?** Not entirely. PAM on Gower distance also separates users mainly by **marital status and sex together**:
- one segment is mostly married women;
- the other is mostly single men, who are somewhat older and earn more.

The two variables are genuinely linked in this sample:

```{r app_sex_married}
round(prop.table(table(sex = app$sex, married = app$married), 1), 2)
```

79% of women are married against 24% of men. The two methods describe this structure differently:
- k-means turns it into exact 100% / 0% partitions on single dummy columns and adds a separate education split;
- PAM shows it as a soft combination of two related traits, with every other variable weighted equally.

## B4. Takeaways

- With mostly categorical data, **k-means on one-hot dummies produces segments that copy individual dummy columns**: here, education level and sex. They are easy to label, but the hard 0% / 100% boundaries come from the encoding, not from the users.
- **Gower distance with PAM** weighs every variable equally, works on the original categories, and gives real, representative users as segment centres. Here it recovers the structure that *is* real, the married-women vs single-men contrast, without the hard partitions. It is the better default for demographic data like this.
- Whichever method is used, the segments should be checked by asking *which variables drive the split* before they are given names.

# Summary

| | Hotel guests | App users |
|---|---|---|
| Data | 9 numeric behavioural variables | 2 binary, 4 categorical, 3 numeric |
| Method | k-means (k = 4, 25 starts) on standardised data | k-means on one-hot data vs Gower + PAM |
| Checks | elbow/silhouette, variable separation, log-transform robustness (ARI) | variable drivers, silhouette, ARI between methods |
| Lesson | separate average from total revenue when targeting; tenure variables are triple-counted | binary dummies can dominate k-means; use a mixed-data distance |
